questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes a boundary of the superior mediastinum?
questions.explanation:
The inferior boundary of the superior mediastinum is the transverse thoracic plane. The superior mediastinum has five boundaries: the manubrium of the sternum anteriorly, vertebral bodies T1–T4 posteriorly, the superior thoracic aperture superiorly, the transverse thoracic plane inferiorly, and the lung pleura laterally. These boundaries define a compact compartment running from the top of the thorax down to the level of the sternal angle.
Option A is incorrect: the anterior boundary is the manubrium, not the xiphoid process. The xiphoid is located at the bottom of the sternum, far inferior to the superior mediastinum.
Option B is incorrect: the posterior boundary is vertebral bodies T1–T4. T5–T8 lie below the transverse thoracic plane, in the posterior mediastinum.
Option D is incorrect: the lateral boundaries are the mediastinal (lung) pleura, not the fibrous pericardium. The pericardium is a structure contained within the mediastinum, not a defining wall of it.

questions.text: A surgical resident uses the transverse thoracic plane (plane of Ludwig) as an anatomical reference during a mediastinal procedure. Which of the following correctly identifies an event that occurs at the level of this plane?
options: The right subclavian artery divides from the brachiocephalic trunk
The pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries
The brachiocephalic veins form by union of the jugular and subclavian veins
The thoracic duct enters the left venous angle
questions.explanation:
The pulmonary trunk divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries at the level of the transverse thoracic plane. The transverse thoracic plane (plane of Ludwig) passes through the sternal angle and marks four simultaneous cardiovascular and respiratory events: the aortic arch begins and ends, the pulmonary trunk bifurcates, the superior vena cava enters the right atrium, and the trachea bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi.
Option A is incorrect: the brachiocephalic trunk divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries at the root of the neck — superior to the transverse thoracic plane, not at it.
Option C is incorrect: the brachiocephalic veins form where the internal jugular and subclavian veins unite at the root of the neck, which is superior to the transverse thoracic plane.
Option D is incorrect: the thoracic duct drains into the left venous angle, the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins, which lies in the neck — well above the transverse thoracic plane.

questions.text: In the superior mediastinum, structures are arranged from anterior to posterior. Which of the following structures lies most anteriorly in this compartment?
questions.explanation:
The thymus is the most anterior structure in the superior mediastinum. From anterior to posterior, the main contents of the superior mediastinum are arranged as: thymus → brachiocephalic veins → SVC → arch of the aorta → trachea → esophagus, with the thoracic duct lying posterolateral to the esophagus. Knowing this anterior-to-posterior order is essential for identifying structures on cross-sectional imaging and predicting which structures an anterior mediastinal mass (such as a thymoma) will compress first.
Option A is incorrect: the esophagus is the most posterior of the major structures listed, lying behind the trachea and anterior to the vertebral bodies.
Option B is incorrect: the trachea lies posterior to the brachiocephalic veins, SVC, and arch of the aorta — it is not the most anterior structure.
Option C is incorrect: the arch of the aorta is posterior to the thymus, both brachiocephalic veins, and the SVC.

questions.text: A 45-year-old woman undergoes CT of the chest after a mass is found incidentally on chest radiograph. The mass occupies the anterior mediastinum, and biopsy confirms the most common neoplasm arising in this compartment. Approximately what proportion of all mediastinal tumors does this neoplasm account for?
questions.explanation:
Thymoma is the most common neoplasm of the anterior mediastinum, accounting for 20–25% of all mediastinal tumors. Within the anterior mediastinum specifically, thymoma accounts for 50% of all anterior mediastinal tumors — but that 50% figure applies only to the anterior compartment, not to all mediastinal compartments combined. Distinguishing these two statistics is a common exam challenge: 20–25% refers to thymoma's share of all mediastinal tumors; 50% refers to its share of anterior mediastinal tumors only. Thymoma is also associated with systemic syndromes, most notably myasthenia gravis.
Option B is incorrect: 40–50% is not the correct proportion of all mediastinal tumors. The 50% figure applies only to the anterior mediastinal compartment, and even then it is the upper end of the stated range — not the proportion of all mediastinal tumors.
Option C is incorrect: 5–10% greatly underestimates thymoma's frequency. It is the predominant mass in the anterior mediastinum.
Option D is incorrect: 50–60% overstates thymoma's share of all mediastinal tumors. The 50% figure is for anterior mediastinal tumors specifically, not for all compartments combined.

questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with a 4-week history of progressive difficulty swallowing and a hoarse voice. Chest imaging reveals a large anterior mediastinal mass. Biopsy confirms thymoma. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of his symptoms?
options: Hematogenous invasion of the esophageal and laryngeal mucosa
questions.explanation:
Thymoma causes local symptoms by directly compressing adjacent structures in the compact superior mediastinum. An expanding thymoma can press against the esophagus (causing dysphagia), the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (causing hoarseness), or the superior vena cava (causing SVC syndrome with facial edema and distended neck veins). Approximately one-third of thymoma patients develop these local compressive symptoms, while one-third to one-half remain completely asymptomatic. Children with thymoma are more likely than adults to present with symptoms.
Option A is incorrect: thymoma produces local symptoms via mass effect and compression, not by hematogenous invasion of mucosal surfaces.
Option B is incorrect: the paraneoplastic mechanism — autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors — underlies myasthenia gravis, a systemic syndrome associated with thymoma. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable proximal muscle weakness and ptosis, not dysphagia from esophageal compression or hoarseness from nerve compression as described here.
Option D is incorrect: lymphatic obstruction causing chylothorax is not a recognized presentation of anterior mediastinal thymoma; it does not explain the dysphagia and hoarseness in this case.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly identifies the two vessels that unite to form each brachiocephalic vein?
options: External jugular vein and cephalic vein
Internal jugular vein and subclavian vein
questions.explanation:
Each brachiocephalic (innominate) vein is formed by the union of the internal jugular vein and the subclavian vein. The internal jugular vein drains the head and neck; the subclavian vein drains the upper extremity. They merge at the base of the neck on each side. In turn, the right and left brachiocephalic veins then unite to form the superior vena cava (SVC = right brachiocephalic + left brachiocephalic).
Option A is incorrect: the cephalic vein is a superficial vein of the lateral arm that drains into the axillary vein, not into the brachiocephalic vein directly.
Option B is incorrect: the external jugular vein is a superficial neck vein that drains into the subclavian vein; neither the external jugular nor the cephalic vein participates in forming the brachiocephalic vein.
Option C is incorrect: the subclavian and axillary veins are the same vessel named differently based on their location (axillary lateral to the first rib, subclavian medial to it) — they are continuous, not two separate vessels that unite.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the formation of the superior vena cava?
options: Union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins
Union of the right internal jugular and subclavian veins
Union of the azygos vein and the right brachiocephalic vein
Union of the internal jugular vein and the thoracic duct
questions.explanation:
The SVC is formed by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins, posterior to the right first costal cartilage. The SVC formation follows a two-step cascade: each internal jugular vein first unites with its ipsilateral subclavian vein to form a brachiocephalic vein, then the two brachiocephalic veins unite to form the SVC. The SVC then descends and enters the right atrium at the level of the transverse thoracic plane, contributing to the right superolateral border of the cardiac silhouette.
Option B is incorrect: the union of the right internal jugular and subclavian veins forms the right brachiocephalic vein — one step upstream from the SVC, not the SVC itself.
Option C is incorrect: the azygos vein is a tributary that drains into the SVC (from behind, at approximately the T4 level) — it does not form the SVC. The azygos system provides collateral drainage when the SVC is obstructed.
Option D is incorrect: the thoracic duct is a lymphatic vessel that drains into the left venous angle at the base of the neck — it is not a blood vessel and has no role in forming the SVC.

questions.text: A radiologist reviewing a frontal chest radiograph identifies the border of the cardiac silhouette that the superior vena cava contributes to. Which border is this?
questions.explanation:
The superior vena cava forms the right superolateral border of the cardiac silhouette. On a frontal chest radiograph, the right border of the cardiac silhouette has two components: the superolateral portion formed by the SVC, and the lower portion formed by the right atrium. On the left, from top to bottom: the aortic knob, the pulmonary artery trunk, the left atrial appendage, and the left ventricle. The SVC enters the right atrium at the level of the transverse thoracic plane, and its straight right-sided course produces the upper right cardiac contour visible on chest X-ray.
Option A is incorrect: the left heart border is formed by the aortic knob, pulmonary artery, left atrial appendage, and left ventricle — the SVC contributes nothing to the left border.
Option B is incorrect: the right inferior border is formed by the right atrium, which sits below the SVC entry point.
Option C is incorrect: the lower right border is the right atrium; the SVC contributes to the upper/superolateral portion of the right cardiac border, not the lower portion.

questions.text: Starting from the first branch (proximal, rightmost) and moving to the third branch (distal, leftmost), which of the following correctly lists the main branches of the aortic arch in order?
options: Left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian
Brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian, left common carotid
Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian
Left subclavian, left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk
questions.explanation:
The three main branches of the aortic arch, in order from proximal (right) to distal (left), are the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery. The brachiocephalic trunk is the largest and most proximal branch; it gives rise to the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries after ascending to the root of the neck. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch and supply the left head/neck and left upper extremity, respectively.
Option A is incorrect: the left common carotid is the second branch, not the first. The brachiocephalic trunk is always the first (and most proximal) branch of the aortic arch.
Option B is incorrect: the left subclavian is the third branch, not the second. The correct middle branch is the left common carotid artery.
Option D is incorrect: this lists the branches in exactly the reverse order — from distal/left to proximal/right — rather than the correct proximal-to-distal sequence.

questions.text: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first branch of the aortic arch. Into which two vessels does it divide, and where does this division occur?
options: Right common carotid and right subclavian, at the root of the neck
Left common carotid and left subclavian, in the superior mediastinum
Right common carotid and right vertebral, at the root of the neck
Right common carotid and right subclavian, within the superior mediastinum
questions.explanation:
The brachiocephalic trunk divides into the right common carotid artery and the right subclavian artery, and this division occurs at the root of the neck — not within the superior mediastinum. The brachiocephalic trunk itself ascends through the superior mediastinum and exits upward into the neck before dividing into its terminal branches. The right common carotid and right subclavian arteries therefore do not reside in the superior mediastinum as individual named vessels.
Option B is incorrect: the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries are the second and third branches of the aortic arch itself — they arise directly from the arch, not from the brachiocephalic trunk. The brachiocephalic trunk gives rise only to right-sided vessels.
Option C is incorrect: the right vertebral artery arises from the right subclavian artery, not directly from the brachiocephalic trunk. The trunk divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian; the vertebral artery is one step further downstream.
Option D is incorrect: the brachiocephalic trunk travels through the superior mediastinum, but the division into the right common carotid and right subclavian occurs after the trunk ascends out of the mediastinum, at the root of the neck.

questions.text: A 3-week-old infant presents with noisy breathing that worsens during both inspiration and expiration, along with feeding difficulties. Imaging confirms a double aortic arch forming a complete vascular ring. Which of the following symptoms is caused specifically by tracheal compression in this condition?
options: Poor feeding and difficulty swallowing liquids
Facial edema and distended neck veins
questions.explanation:
Inspiratory and expiratory stridor is caused by tracheal compression in a double aortic arch vascular ring. A double aortic arch forms a complete vascular ring encircling both the trachea and esophagus. Tracheal compression produces respiratory symptoms: inspiratory and expiratory stridor, expiratory wheeze, hoarse cry, and in severe cases, blue baby (marked cyanosis). Esophageal compression produces a separate symptom set: poor feeding, difficulty swallowing liquids, regurgitation, and choking. Distinguishing tracheal from esophageal symptoms allows localization of the ring's most critical dimension for surgical planning.
Option A is incorrect: poor feeding and difficulty swallowing liquids result from esophageal compression by the vascular ring — not tracheal compression.
Option C is incorrect: regurgitation and choking are also esophageal compression symptoms. The esophagus lies posterior to the trachea in the ring; these symptoms arise from its compression, not from airway compromise.
Option D is incorrect: facial edema and distended neck veins are signs of superior vena cava syndrome from SVC obstruction, which is an entirely different mechanism unrelated to a double aortic arch vascular ring.

questions.text: During laboratory dissection of the superior mediastinum, a student traces the left vagus nerve as it descends through the thorax. At which anatomical landmark does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve branch from the left vagus nerve?
options: At the posterior aspect of the sternal angle
Medial to the left brachiocephalic vein
Anterior to the left main bronchus
questions.explanation:
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the left vagus nerve posterolateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. As the left vagus nerve descends through the superior mediastinum, it descends along the left side of the aortic arch and, as it reaches the underside of the arch, gives off the left recurrent laryngeal nerve at a point posterolateral to the ligamentum arteriosum — the fibrous remnant of the ductus arteriosus connecting the left pulmonary artery to the undersurface of the aortic arch. The nerve then loops under the arch and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove to reach the larynx.
Option A is incorrect: the sternal angle marks the transverse thoracic plane on the surface, where the aortic arch begins and ends. It is a surface landmark, not the branching point of the left RLN; the nerve branches at the underside of the arch, not at the sternal angle itself.
Option B is incorrect: the left brachiocephalic vein lies anterior and superior to the aortic arch, crossing anteriorly over the arch branches. The RLN branches inferolaterally, at the underside of the arch near the ligamentum arteriosum — not medial to the brachiocephalic vein.
Option C is incorrect: the left main bronchus passes inferior to the aortic arch after the tracheal bifurcation at the transverse thoracic plane. The RLN branches from the vagus posterolateral to the ligamentum arteriosum, not anterior to the bronchus.

questions.text: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of the aorta. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve follows a different course because no aortic arch equivalent exists on the right side. Under which structure does the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loop?
questions.explanation:
The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the right subclavian artery. This left-right asymmetry reflects embryologic aortic arch remodeling: on the left, the nerve loops under the arch of the aorta (a left-sided structure); on the right, with no corresponding persistent arch, the nerve loops instead around the right subclavian artery. Both nerves then ascend in the tracheoesophageal groove to reach the larynx. Clinically, this explains why left-sided mediastinal pathology (arch aneurysm, left lung malignancy, mediastinal lymphadenopathy) selectively injures the left RLN, while pathology near the right subclavian territory injures the right RLN.
Option A is incorrect: the arch of the aorta is where the LEFT recurrent laryngeal nerve loops — not the right. The aorta is a left-sided structure, and there is no right aortic arch equivalent in normal anatomy.
Option C is incorrect: the right common carotid artery arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and ascends in the neck; the right RLN loops under the right subclavian artery specifically, not the common carotid.
Option D is incorrect: the brachiocephalic trunk bifurcates into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The right RLN loops under the right subclavian — a terminal branch of the trunk — not the undivided trunk itself.

questions.text: A 62-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents with a 6-week history of progressive hoarseness. Laryngoscopy reveals paralysis of the left vocal cord, and his wife reports that his cough has sounded weak for the past month. Damage to which of the following nerves best explains this constellation of findings?
questions.explanation:
Hoarse voice, left vocal cord paralysis, and weak cough are the classic findings of left recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. The left RLN supplies motor innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. Palsy produces an immobile left vocal cord (paralysis), a breathy or hoarse voice from incomplete glottic closure, and a weak, ineffective cough because the patient cannot build sufficient intrathoracic pressure with a paralyzed cord. In a heavy smoker, causes include bronchogenic carcinoma, aortic arch aneurysm, and enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes — all compressing the nerve along its course through the superior mediastinum.
Option A is incorrect: the left vagus nerve is the parent of the left RLN, but vagus nerve damage produces far wider deficits — impaired swallowing (pharyngeal branches), loss of gag reflex, autonomic effects on heart rate, and GI dysfunction — far beyond isolated hoarseness and weak cough.
Option B is incorrect: the left phrenic nerve (C3–C5) innervates the left hemidiaphragm. Its palsy causes left hemidiaphragm elevation and may cause exertional dyspnea, but it does not affect the vocal cords or cough clearance mechanism.
Option D is incorrect: the superior laryngeal nerve (internal and external branches) affects pitch control (cricothyroid) and supraglottic sensation; its palsy changes voice pitch and reduces laryngeal sensation above the cords, but it does not cause complete vocal cord paralysis or the weak cough pattern described here.

questions.text: A 71-year-old man with longstanding hypertension and a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a 3-week history of hoarseness. He reports no fever, sore throat, or recent respiratory illness. Chest CT reveals a large aneurysm of the aortic arch. Against which adjacent structure is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve compressed in this setting?
questions.explanation:
In an aortic arch aneurysm, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is compressed against the left pulmonary artery. The left RLN passes through the aortopulmonary window — a tight space between the undersurface of the aortic arch and the top of the left pulmonary artery. When an arch aneurysm expands, the nerve is trapped between the bulging arch and the left pulmonary artery, producing a stretch injury or direct compression. Hoarseness can be the only presenting symptom of an aortic arch aneurysm, which makes recognizing this association clinically important: unexplained hoarseness in an appropriate patient should prompt chest imaging.
Option B is incorrect: the left brachiocephalic vein passes anterior to the roots of the aortic arch branches, superior and anterior to the region of the aneurysm. It is not the structure against which the nerve is trapped in the aortopulmonary window.
Option C is incorrect: the trachea lies posterior to the aortic arch and could be impinged by a large aneurysm, potentially causing stridor, but the nerve is compressed against the left pulmonary artery specifically in the aortopulmonary window — not the trachea.
Option D is incorrect: the esophagus lies posterior to the trachea, removed from the aortopulmonary window. A very large aneurysm might secondarily compress the esophagus (causing dysphagia), but the specific mechanism for RLN compression in an arch aneurysm involves the left pulmonary artery.

questions.text: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a 3-week history of progressive facial swelling and shortness of breath. Examination reveals marked facial edema, multiple dilated veins across his neck and anterior chest wall, and mild dyspnea. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of these findings?
options: Reduced cardiac output from left ventricular systolic dysfunction
Elevated venous pressure from cardiac tamponade
Lymphatic obstruction at the level of the thoracic duct
Partial obstruction of the superior vena cava
questions.explanation:
Facial edema, distended neck and chest wall veins, and dyspnea are the classic signs of superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS), caused by partial obstruction of the SVC. The SVC drains venous blood from the head, neck, and upper extremities into the right atrium. When the SVC is partially obstructed — most commonly by a malignant tumor, especially lung cancer of the right lung — venous pressure rises in all upstream structures. The result is dependent facial and upper extremity edema, visible engorgement and distension of neck and chest wall veins, and dyspnea from increased intrathoracic venous pressure.
Option A is incorrect: reduced left ventricular output causes systemic hypoperfusion — low blood pressure, cool extremities, and fatigue — not the venous engorgement pattern seen here. Low cardiac output does not produce facial edema or visibly distended thoracic wall veins in isolation.
Option B is incorrect: cardiac tamponade raises central venous pressure and can cause jugular venous distension, but it presents with Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension) and typically pulsus paradoxus — not the predominantly facial and thoracic wall venous engorgement distribution of SVC syndrome.
Option C is incorrect: thoracic duct obstruction causes chylothorax or lower-body lymphedema — not the superior distribution (face, neck, chest wall) that characterizes SVC obstruction.
